name: Chasok Tangnam
summary: Chasok Tangnam is the harvest festival of the Limbu (Yakthung) people, held on the full moon of Mangsir. Families offer the first grain of the new harvest to Yuma Sammang and other deities, priests recite the Mundhum, and communities gather to eat, dance and visit one another.
body: In the Limbu year, the rice and millet harvest is not complete until the first of it has been offered back. Chasok Tangnam falls on the full moon of Mangsir, in the Limbu calendar the month of Senchengla, usually in late November or December. On this day families offer new grain and other first fruits of the harvest to Yuma Sammang, the ancestral goddess of the Limbu, and to other deities and ancestors.

The rituals are led by Limbu priests, such as the phedangma, who recite passages of the Mundhum, the oral scripture that holds Limbu history, law and ritual. The words are chanted, not read, and some passages are long. Offerings are made in homes and at community gatherings, and blessings are shared with relatives.

Then the celebration begins: food made from the new harvest, tongba and other drinks, and dances such as the chyabrung drum dance and the dhan nach, the paddy dance of slow, linked circles. In Ilam, Taplejung, Panchthar, Tehrathum and Dhankuta, and in Limbu communities in cities, people gather in traditional dress. The same full moon is also Udhauli for other Kirat communities.
tips: Ask our guide to find out where community gatherings are held that year; they are usually in villages and community halls rather than fixed sites.
Watch quietly during the Mundhum recitation and offerings, and ask before photographing priests or rituals.
Accept food and drink with your right hand; it is fine to decline tongba politely if you do not drink.

faqs.a: Chasok Tangnam falls on the full moon of the Nepali month of Mangsir, which is usually in late November or December. The date changes each year with the lunar calendar. Check current dates before you travel, as local gatherings may be held on the day or nearby weekends.

Chasok Tangnam is celebrated by the Limbu (Yakthung) people, a Kirat community of eastern Nepal and of Sikkim and Darjeeling in India. In Nepal it is most visible in Limbu districts such as Taplejung, Panchthar, Ilam, Tehrathum and Dhankuta.

Yes, visitors are generally welcome at community gatherings when they come with a local guide or host and behave as guests. Rituals in family homes are private unless you are invited. Dress modestly, ask before taking photographs and follow your hosts' lead.

Families and priests offer the first grain and fruits of the harvest to Yuma Sammang and other deities while passages of the Mundhum are recited. Afterwards, people share food made from the new harvest, drink tongba, visit relatives and dance, including the chyabrung drum dance and the dhan nach.

name: Sakela (Ubhauli and Udhauli)
when: Twice a year: Baisakh full moon (Ubhauli, April–May) and Mangsir full moon (Udhauli, November–December)
summary: Sakela, also called Sakewa or Sakenwa, is the main festival of the Kirat Rai. It is held twice a year: Ubhauli at the Baisakh full moon, when people and animals move up to the hills and planting begins, and Udhauli at the Mangsir full moon, after the harvest, when they move down. Large circles of dancers mark both.
body: Sakela follows the farming year and the seasonal movement of people, animals and birds. Ubhauli, meaning going up, falls on the Baisakh full moon in spring, when the weather warms and the planting season starts. Udhauli, going down, falls on the Mangsir full moon in late autumn, after the harvest, when the cold begins. Both are described in the Mundhum, the oral tradition shared by Kirat peoples.

At the heart of Sakela is the dance. Men and women in traditional dress form a large circle, often around a sacred site or ritual stones, and move to the beat of the dhol drum and jhyamta cymbals. Each step, called a sili, imitates the movement of birds, animals or farm work such as sowing and harvesting. Different Rai groups have their own steps, and a ritual leader opens the dance with prayers and offerings.

Sakela is celebrated across the Rai hills of eastern Nepal and in towns where Rai people live, including Dhankuta, Dharan, Bhojpur, Khotang and Kathmandu. Community grounds fill with families, food stalls and visitors. In Dhankuta, gatherings are held in several places around the district.
tips: Arrive in the early afternoon; the main dancing often builds through the afternoon after the rituals.
Watch first and join the outer circle only if invited; follow the steps of the dancers next to you.
Ask before photographing rituals, priests or individuals, and do not walk through the middle of the circle.

faqs.a: Twice a year. Sakela Ubhauli is on the Baisakh full moon, usually late April or May, and Sakela Udhauli is on the Mangsir full moon, usually late November or December. Dates follow the lunar calendar and change each year; check current dates before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Ubhauli and Udhauli?
faqs.a: Ubhauli means going up and marks spring, when people, animals and birds move to higher ground and planting begins. Udhauli means going down and marks late autumn, after the harvest, when they move to lower, warmer ground. Both are celebrated with the Sakela dance.

faqs.q: Where can I see Sakela in eastern Nepal?
faqs.a: Sakela is held across the Rai hills, including Dhankuta, Bhojpur, Khotang, Dharan and many villages, and in cities such as Kathmandu. In Dhankuta, gatherings take place at several community grounds. We find out the main local sites each year before your trip.

faqs.q: Can visitors dance in the Sakela circle?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Visitors are usually welcome to watch, and dancers sometimes invite guests into the circle. Wait to be invited, follow the steps of those beside you, and do not interrupt the ritual part led by the priest at the start.

name: Pathibhara Pilgrimage Seasons
when: Busiest around Dashain (Sept–Oct) and Chaite Dashain (March–April); pilgrims come all year
summary: Pilgrims climb to Pathibhara Devi, the hilltop goddess shrine at 3,794 m above Taplejung, all year round, but numbers peak around the two Navaratri seasons: Bada Dashain in autumn and Chaite Dashain in spring. Thousands of devotees from Nepal and India make the climb, many fulfilling vows.
body: Pathibhara Devi, known in Limbu as Mukkumlung, is one of the most important goddess shrines in eastern Nepal. Pilgrims believe that a sincere visit brings wishes to fulfilment, and many come to make a vow, a bhakal, and return later to repay it with an offering.

The busiest times are the nine nights of Navaratri that lead up to Dashain in late September or October, and Chaite Dashain in March or April, both seasons devoted to the goddess Durga. In these weeks the road head below the hill, the trail and the summit are crowded, queues at the shrine can last hours, and lodges in Phungling and near the trail fill up. Many pilgrims come from Jhapa, Morang and Sunsari in the plains, and from Sikkim, Darjeeling and further into India.

Outside these peaks, October and November remain popular for the clear weather and mountain views, and spring brings rhododendrons. Winter snow can make the climb hard, and the monsoon brings rain and cloud.
tips: If you want the atmosphere, go during Navaratri; if you want calm, go a few weeks before or after.
Book lodges in Phungling and near the trailhead well ahead for Dashain and Chaite Dashain.
Start the climb before dawn to beat both the queues and the late-morning cloud.

faqs.a: Pathibhara is busiest during Navaratri before Dashain, usually late September or October, and Chaite Dashain in March or April. Public holidays and Saturdays in spring and autumn are busy too. Dates move each year with the lunar calendar; check current dates before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it worth visiting Pathibhara during Dashain?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to see the pilgrimage at its most intense, with crowds of devotees, bells and offerings. Be ready for long queues, full lodges and higher prices. For a quieter visit with the same weather, go in November.

faqs.q: Can I visit Pathibhara in winter?
faqs.a: Pilgrims do visit in winter, but December to February brings cold and possible snow on the upper trail, which can make the climb slippery or close it for days. Go with a guide, bring proper winter gear and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does a Pathibhara pilgrimage take from the plains?
faqs.a: From Jhapa or Biratnagar, most pilgrims take three to four days: a long drive to Phungling, a night near the trailhead, the climb and descent, and the drive back. From Kathmandu, add a flight to Bhadrapur or Biratnagar.
